newsitem.title: UK: Grobbelaar witness says he counted rigging money.
newsitem.headline: Grobbelaar witness says he counted rigging money.

text.p: Former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar received a 40,000 pound ($65,000) pay-off for rigging a match in November 1993, the chief prosecution witness in his trial said on Monday.
Chris Vincent told the trial of Grobbelaar and three others the goalkeeper told him to count the money he received after he and striker John Fashanu attended a meeting in north London.
While Vincent waited in the car, the two footballers went into a house in north London. Grobbelaar came out and told him to open an envelope in his briefcase, Vincent said.
"I opened the envelope, counted the money, it was all in 50 pound notes, there was 40,000 pounds there. I confirmed to Mr Grobbelaar there was 40,000 pounds," he told the court.
Vincent, the first witness to testify in the case, said Grobbelaar chose to throw the game against Newcastle after talking to an Asian middleman the keeper called the "Short Man."

"In the weekend leading up to the Newcastle game, after one of the calls to the Short Man, Grobbelaar said to me: "I'm doing the business this weekend'," said Vincent, who like Grobbelaar comes from Zimbabwe.
Grobbelaar is accused of fixing matches with the help of Fashanu and Malaysian businessmen Heng Suan Lim, who both received large cash sums from Asia.
Neither could explain where the money had come from, the court heard. The prosecution says the "Short Man" is Lim and telephone records show the two men talked frequently before soccer matches.
"Grobbelaar told me that John Fashanu had made somewhere between 400,000 pounds and 800,000 pounds during business with the Short Man," Vincent told the court.

Vincent, who exchanged several long glances with Grobbelaar across the court room before giving evidence, said the footballer got in his car after the game, which Newcastle won 3-0, and said "Good result".
Grobbelaar, who had a passenger with him, replied "Ja" (yes) but said nothing else.
"To me personally he said he was going to collect the money," said Vincent, adding that he flew down to London the following Thursday with the keeper to pick up the money.

Vincent, a former business associate of Grobbelaar, helped break the story in November 1994 when he covertly recorded the keeper admitting he had tried to throw games. He then handed over the tapes to the Sun tabloid newspaper.
Vincent, in prison on another matter, said Grobbelaar decided to fix games because he was unhappy at being paid less than some newcomers to the Liverpool team.

In the middle of 1993 Grobbelaar said Fashanu had introduced him to men from the Far East who were prepared to pay 1,500 to 2,000 pounds a week for predicting the outcome of soccer games, Vincent told the court, adding that the keeper then decided to go further.

"You know the people I talked to from the Far East? I will meet one of them and we're going to discuss getting paid for fixing soccer games," Vincent quoted Grobbelaar as saying. Vincent then asked how this could be done.
"He said he'd been the Liverpool keeper for 14 years and if he was standing a foot off his line nobody would know."
The other man on trial is former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers, accused with Lim and Fashanu of taking part in a separate bid to fix matches.
All four pleaded not guilty to the charges which carry seven-year prison sentences and unlimited fines. ($1=.6021 Pound)
